In Proposition 1 we provide the canonical gradients for three estimands $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:tau_{i}d}\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}=\mathbb{E}[\tau(x;m)\mid S=1];\quad\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}=\mathbb{E}[\tau(x;m)\mid S=0];\quad\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}=\mathbb{E}[\tau(x;m)] $$

in the data fusion setting where $R=(S,Z,X)$ . Recall that $\tau(x;m)=m_{11}(x)-m_{10}(x)$ is the conditional average treatment effect when treatment is randomized (conditional on $X$ ) in the experiment. In that case, $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ identifies the average treatment effect for the population of subjects from which the experimental dataset is sampled. Under an additional mean-exchangeability assumption on the potential outcomes, Dahabreh et al. (2019); Dahabreh et al. (2020) show that $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ identify the average treatment effect in the population defined by the observational dataset and the fused dataset, respectively, as long as the RCT selection probability $p(x)=\textnormal{Pr}(S=1\mid X=x)$ is bounded away from 0. We do not discuss specific identification assumptions further, as our focus is on improving precision via restrictions on the outcome mean function $m$ for already identified estimands.

#### Proposition 1.

The efficient influence functions $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ for the estimands $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ defined in (9) at the true observed data distribution $P^{*}$ in the nonparametric model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{R}}$ are given by

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*},\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=\frac{s(\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})+m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*})}{\rho^{*}} \displaystyle\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=\frac{s(1-p^{*}(x))\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})}{p^{*}(x)(1-\rho^{*})}+\frac{(1-s)(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*})}{1-\rho^{*}} \displaystyle\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}^{*},\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=\frac{s}{p^{*}(x)}\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})+m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}^{*} $$

where the components of $\eta^{*}=\eta^{*}(\cdot)=(m^{*}(1,\cdot,\cdot),e^{*}(\cdot),p^{*}(\cdot))$ are defined in Table 1 and $\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})$ is the inverse propensity weighted difference

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:Delta}\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})=\frac{z(y-m_{11}^{*}(x))}{e^{*}(x)}-\frac{(1-z)(y-m_{10}^{*}(x))}{1-e^{*}(x)}. $$

#### Proof.

Equation (10) is from Section 2.2 of Li et al. (2023b). Equations (11) and (12) are from Theorem 2.3 of Li et al. (2023a). ∎

As noted in the introduction, the AIPW estimator of Robins et al. (1994), among many other popular estimators for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , attains the influence function $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ without using any observational data. Reweighted variants of AIPW, referred to as augmented inverse propensity of sampling weighting (AIPSW) estimators by Colnet et al. (2024), attain the influence functions $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ and $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , respectively, using the experimental data along with the covariates (but not the outcomes) in the observational data.

### 2.2 The outcome mean function tangent space

If the set $\mathcal{M}$ is a closed linear space, the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ is simply $\mathcal{M}$ .

#### Proposition 2.

If $\mathcal{M}$ is a closed linear subspace of $\mathcal{H}_{R}$ , then $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathcal{M}$ .

#### Proof.

First suppose $f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . Then there exists a sequence of nonrandom vectors $\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ and outcome mean function parametric submodels $\{M_{\gamma}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ such that the functions

$$ f_{i}=c_{i}^{\top}\frac{\partial M_{\gamma}^{(i)}}{\partial\gamma}\Bigg|_{\gamma=0} $$

converge in mean square to $f$ . But for each $i$ , letting $s_{i}$ be the dimension of $c_{i}$ we have

$$ c^{\top}\frac{\partial M_{\gamma}^{(i)}(\cdot)}{\partial\gamma}\Bigg|_{\gamma=0}=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\sum_{k=1}^{s_{i}}c_{k}\frac{M_{he_{k}}(\cdot)-m^{*}(\cdot)}{h} $$

is a limit of linear combinations of functions in $\mathcal{M}$ , hence still in $\mathcal{M}$ due to $\mathcal{M}$ being closed and linear. Above, $e_{k}$ denotes the $k$ -th standard basis vector in $\real{}^{s_{i}}$ . We conclude $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}$ .

To show the reverse inclusion, note that for any $f\in\mathcal{M}$ we can write $f$ as the derivative of the one-dimensional parametric submodel $m(\cdot;\gamma)=m^{*}(\cdot)+\gamma f(\cdot)$ , which is indeed a submodel as it satisfies $m(\cdot;\gamma)\in\mathcal{M}$ for all $\gamma$ due to $\mathcal{M}$ being a linear space. ∎

It is straightforward to verify that the collections $\mathcal{M}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{4}$ of (1) and 3, respectively, are in fact closed linear spaces, so that $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}=\mathcal{M}_{i}$ for $i=2,4$ . A linear restricted moment model $\mathcal{M}=\{r\mapsto\psi(r)^{\top}\beta\mid\beta\in\real^{q}\}$ , a special case of $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ in Example 1, is also a closed linear space.

In other cases, computing the space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ may require some more work. However, Theorem 2 ensures that computing $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ (and its orthogonal complement) can replace the work of directly deriving the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . Such a direct derivation generally requires reasoning about integral restrictions on log likelihoods in parametric submodels. The proof of Theorem 2 essentially proceeds by working out such reasoning for general $\mathcal{M}$ so that the user only needs to reason about the space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , which requires only considering derivatives of outcome mean function submodels.

To illustrate this, we work through a novel derivation of the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ , where $\mathcal{M}_{5}$ is the outcome mean function collection (5) in the outcome-mediated selection bias setting of Example 5.

#### Example 6 (continues=ex:outcome_selection_bias).

Let $\ell(x)=\log(x)-\log(1-x)$ be the logistic link function, so that (4) can be written as

$$ \ell(m_{11}(x))=\ell(m_{10}(x))+\ell(m_{01}(x))-\ell(m_{00}(x)). $$

Essentially, the restriction (4) allows $m_{10}$ , $m_{01}$ , and $m_{00}$ to freely vary but then $m_{11}$ is a deterministic function of $(m_{10},m_{01},m_{00})$ . Thus, a generic outcome mean function parametric submodel for $\mathcal{M}_{5}$ takes the form

$$ \displaystyle m_{sz}(x;\gamma) \displaystyle=szf_{11}(x;\gamma)+s(1-z)f_{10}(x;\gamma_{10})+(1-s)zf_{01}(x;\gamma_{01})+(1-s)(1-z)f_{00}(x;\gamma_{00}) \displaystyle f_{11}(x;\gamma) \displaystyle=\ell^{-1}[\ell(f_{10}(x;\gamma_{10}))+\ell(f_{01}(x;\gamma_{01}))-\ell(f_{00}(x;\gamma_{00}))] $$

for $\gamma=(\gamma_{10}^{\top},\gamma_{01}^{\top},\gamma_{00}^{\top})^{\top}\in\real^{s}$ . For any $c=(c_{10}^{\top},c_{01}^{\top},c_{00}^{\top})^{\top}\in\real^{r}$ partitioned as $\gamma$ , we compute

$$ \displaystyle c^{\top}\frac{\partial m(r;\gamma)}{\partial\gamma}\Big|_{\gamma=0} \displaystyle=[s(1-z)+sz\kappa^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))]c_{10}^{\top}f_{10}^{\prime}(x;0) \displaystyle\quad+[(1-s)z+sz\kappa^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))]c_{01}^{\top}f_{01}^{\prime}(x;0) \displaystyle\quad+[(1-s)(1-z)-sz\kappa^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))]c_{00}^{\top}f_{00}^{\prime}(x;0) $$

where $f_{j}^{\prime}(x;a)\equiv\partial f_{j}(x;\alpha)/\partial\alpha|_{\alpha=a}$ for $j\in\{10,01,00\}$ and $\kappa^{*}(x)=(\ell^{-1})^{\prime}[\ell(m_{11}^{*}(x))]=(\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}^{*}(x)))^{-1}$ . We note the preceding display is of the form

$$ s(1-z)g_{1}(x)+(1-s)zg_{2}(x)+(1-s)(1-z)g_{3}(x)+sz\kappa^{*}(x)[\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))g_{1}(x)+\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))g_{2}(x)-\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))g_{3}(x)] $$

for some $g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ and hypothesize that any function of this form lies in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ .

To show this, we fix arbitrary $g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ and note there exists an outcome mean function submodel $m(r;\gamma)$ of the form in (14) and (15) with

$$ \displaystyle f_{10}(x;\gamma_{10}) \displaystyle=m_{10}^{*}(x)+\gamma_{10}g_{1}(x) \displaystyle f_{01}(x;\gamma_{01}) \displaystyle=m_{01}^{*}(x)+\gamma_{01}g_{2}(x) \displaystyle f_{00}(x;\gamma_{00}) \displaystyle=m_{00}^{*}(x)+\gamma_{00}g_{3}(x) $$

where $\gamma=(\gamma_{10},\gamma_{01},\gamma_{00})\in\real^{3}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle(1,1,1)^{\top}\frac{\partial m_{sz}(x;\gamma)}{\partial\gamma}\Big|_{\gamma=0}=s(1-z)g_{1}(x)+(1-s)zg_{2}(x)+(1-s)(1-z)g_{3}(x)+sz\kappa^{*}(x)\iota^{*}(x) $$

which shows that indeed,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}= \displaystyle\{r\mapsto s(1-z)g_{1}(x)+(1-s)zg_{2}(x)+(1-s)(1-z)g_{3}(x) \displaystyle\quad+sz\kappa^{*}(x)[\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))g_{1}(x)+\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))g_{2}(x)-\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))g_{3}(x)]\mid g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}. $$

### 2.3 Orthogonal complements and projections

The final step in deriving the EIF is to compute the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ of the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ along with the projection (7). A useful way to compute $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ is to characterize it as the set of all functions in $\mathcal{H}_{R}$ whose projection onto $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ is zero. We compute such projections, as well as the final projection (7), by using the law of iterated expectations to write the projection objective as a function of $X$ solely, and then minimize the objective using calculus. We perform both these steps for the collection $\mathcal{M}_{5}$ below.

#### Example 7 (continues=ex:outcome_selection_bias).

By definition, the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}$ of the set $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ in (16) consists of all functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which the projection $\pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}})$ is zero. By (16), an arbitrary function in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ takes the form

$$ \displaystyle\iota(x;g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}) \displaystyle=s(1-z)g_{1}(x)+(1-s)zg_{2}(x)+(1-s)(1-z)g_{3}(x)+sz\upsilon^{*}(x;g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}) \displaystyle\upsilon^{*}(x;g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}) \displaystyle=\kappa^{*}(x)[\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))g_{1}(x)+\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))g_{2}(x)-\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))g_{3}(x)] $$

for some $(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{3}$ . Then for any $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ , we have $\pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}})(x)=\iota(x;h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})$ where $(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})$ minimize the projection objective

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(h(R)-\iota(X;g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))^{2}] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-\upsilon^{*}(X;g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))^{2}\Big]+\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(h_{10}(X)-g_{1}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-g_{2}(X))^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))(1-q^{*}(X))(h_{00}(X)-g_{3}(X))^{2}] $$

over $(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{3}$ , where the second equality follows from writing

$$ h(R)=SZh_{11}(X)+S(1-Z)h_{10}(X)+(1-S)Zh_{01}(X)+(1-S)(1-Z)h_{00}(X) $$

and conditioning on $X$ , and we have used the notation from Table 1. With the objective now solely an expectation of a function of $X$ , we can compute the optimizers $(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})$ simply by minimizing the argument of the expectation pointwise in $(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})$ . This yields the first-order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(h_{11}(x)-\upsilon^{*}(x;h_{1},h_{2},h_{3}))\kappa^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))-p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))(h_{10}(x)-g_{1}(x)) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(h_{11}(x)-\upsilon^{*}(x;h_{1},h_{2},h_{3}))\kappa^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))-(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)(h_{01}(x)-g_{2}(x)) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(h_{11}(x)-\upsilon^{*}(x;h_{1},h_{2},h_{3}))\kappa^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))-(1-p^{*}(x))(1-q^{*}(x))(h_{00}(x)-g_{3}(x)) $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . We conclude $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}$ is the set of all $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which $h_{1}=h_{2}=h_{3}=0$ solves this system of equations. This is precisely the functions $h$ satisfying

$$ \displaystyle(1-e^{*}(x))h_{10}(x) \displaystyle=-e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x)\frac{\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))}{\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}^{*}(x))} \displaystyle(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)h_{01}(x) \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x)\frac{\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))}{\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}^{*}(x))} \displaystyle(1-p^{*}(x))(1-q^{*}(x))h_{00}(x) \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x)\frac{\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))}{\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}^{*}(x))} $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Noting that (17), (18), and (19) determine $h_{10}$ , $h_{01}$ , and $h_{00}$ in terms of $h_{11}$ and letting $\zeta(x)$ denote $h_{11}(x)/\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}^{*}(x))$ , we can write this succinctly as

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}=\{f^{*}(r)\zeta(x)\mid\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\} $$

for $f^{*}(r)\equiv f(r;\eta^{*})$ where

$$ \displaystyle f(r;\eta) \displaystyle=sz\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}(x))-\frac{s(1-z)e(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}(x))}{1-e(x)} \displaystyle\quad-\frac{(1-s)zp(x)e(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}(x))}{(1-p(x))q(x)}+\frac{(1-s)(1-z)p(x)e(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}(x))}{(1-p(x))(1-q(x))} $$

and the nuisance parameters are $\eta(\cdot)=(p(\cdot),e(\cdot),q(\cdot),m(\cdot))$ . We conclude via (8) that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:T_{M}{}_{p}erp_{o}utcome_{s}election_{b}ias}\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto f^{*}(r)\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(r))\mid\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}. $$

Finally, to derive the EIF we perform the projection (7). This amounts to solving the optimization problem

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:outcome_{s}election_{b}ias_{p}rojection}\min_{\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-f^{*}(R)\zeta(X)(Y-m^{*}(R))\right)^{2}\right] $$

Similar to our derivation of the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}$ , we perform this minimization by re-writing the objective via conditioning on $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-f^{*}(R)\zeta(X)(Y-m^{*}(R))\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left[\zeta(X)^{2}\mathbb{E}[f^{*}(R)^{2}(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}\mid X]-2\zeta(X)\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})f^{*}(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X]\right]+const. $$

Minimizing the argument of the expectation shows the solution to (22) is $\zeta(\cdot;\eta^{*})\equiv\zeta(\cdot;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})$ where

$$ \zeta(x;\eta)\equiv\zeta(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})=\frac{\int\varphi_{0}(w;\tau,\eta)f(r;\eta)(y-m(r))dP_{(S,Z,Y\mid X)}(s,z,y;x)}{\int f(r;\eta)^{2}(y-m(r))^{2}dP_{(S,Z,Y\mid X)}(s,z,y;x)} $$

and so by (7) the EIF is

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:outcome_{s}election_{b}ias_{e}if}\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-f(r;\eta^{*})\zeta(x;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})(y-m^{*}(r)). $$

### 2.4 Additional insights

Commonly, the propensity score $e^{*}(x)$ in the experimental dataset is known, as it is subject to the control of the investigator. Hahn (1998) famously showed that knowledge of the propensity score does not change the semiparametric efficiency bound for estimating $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ relative to the nonparametric model. This may not be true in general, however, for other estimands or for proper semiparametric models like $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ .

We can readily extend Theorem 2 to characterize the space of influence functions of RAL estimators in the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ that imposes the restriction $e(x)=e^{*}(x)$ for some known function $e^{*}(\cdot)$ in addition to the outcome mean function restriction that $m\in\mathcal{M}$ . The main insight is to note that with $e(x)=\textnormal{Pr}(Z=1\mid S=1,X=x)=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid S=1,X=x]$ , a known experimental propensity score can be viewed as a restriction on the outcome mean function of the observations $(Z,S,X)$ , where now $Z$ is viewed as the “outcome” and $(S,X)$ are the covariates. Such a restriction is variationally independent of any outcome mean function restriction on the original dataset (i.e., that $m\in\mathcal{M}$ ), which must pertain to the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $(Z,S,X)$ . This allows us to recursively apply Theorem 2. Similar ideas could be used to characterize semiparametric efficiency when either instead of or in addition to a known experimental propensity score, the RCT selection probability $p^{*}(x)$ is known, as in a nested trial setup where RCT participants are directly sampled from a larger group by the investigator. A known selection probability is a restriction on the conditional mean of $S$ given $X$ , which is variationally independent of any restrictions on the conditional distribution of $Z$ given $(S,X)$ (e.g., known experimental propensity score), or on the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $R$ (e.g., that $m\in\mathcal{M}$ ).

#### Corollary 1.

Suppose the conditions of Theorem 2 are satisfied for some outcome mean function collection $\mathcal{M}$ in the causal inference setting where $R=(S,Z,X)\in\{0,1\}^{2}\times\mathcal{X}$ . Then $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , the orthogonal complement in $\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}$ of the semiparametric tangent space $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ for the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ that imposes the restrictions that $m\in\mathcal{M}$ and $\textnormal{Pr}(Z=1\mid S=1,X=x)=e^{*}(x)$ for known $e^{*}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ , satisfies

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\oplus\left\{w\mapsto sh(x)(z-e^{*}(x))\Big|h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\right\}.\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:T_{M}{}_{p}erp_{t}ilde} $$

#### Proof.

See Appendix A.3. ∎

Theorem 2 can also provide useful insight into when certain modeling assumptions may not be helpful, in the sense that imposing such restrictions cannot improve (decrease) the semiparametric efficiency bound.

#### Corollary 2.

Suppose the experimental propensity score is constant, i.e. $e^{*}(x)=e^{*}\in(0,1)$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , and the variance functions in the RCT are homoskedastic, i.e.

$$ V^{*}(1,z,x)=\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid S=1,Z=z,X=x)=\sigma_{z}^{2},\quad z\in\{0,1\},x\in\mathcal{X} $$

for some positive constants $\sigma_{0}^{2}$ and $\sigma_{1}^{2}$ . Additionally, suppose $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{R}$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2 and the corresponding outcome mean tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ contains all functions $m$ for which $m_{11}$ and $m_{10}$ are arbitrary constants and $m_{01}$ and $m_{00}$ are identically zero. Then $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ , the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ in the nonparametric model given in (10), is also the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ in both $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ .

#### Proof.

See Appendix A.4. ∎

To understand the implications of Corollary 2, consider the following restrictive set of modeling assumptions: the outcome mean functions $m_{01}$ and $m_{00}$ in the observational dataset are known exactly, while the outcome mean functions $m_{11}$ and $m_{10}$ in the RCT are linear in some known low-dimensional basis functions $\psi(x)$ containing an intercept. It is straightforward to show that the set $\mathcal{M}$ of permissible outcome mean functions under these restrictions satisfies the conditions of Corollary 2. This shows that with homoskedastic outcomes and a constant propensity score $e^{*}$ , even very stringent assumptions on the outcome mean functions do not enable any asymptotic improvement over the AIPW estimator for estimating $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ . The same automatically applies for any set of strictly less stringent assumptions, such as the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ (again assuming $\psi(x)$ contains an intercept). Recall that the AIPW estimator neither uses any information from the observational dataset nor places any parametric or semiparametric assumptions on the outcome mean functions. Thus, Corollary 2 shows it is not useful in large samples to make such assumptions to try and leverage the observational data if we have a constant RCT propensity score and expect homoskedastic outcomes. Conversely, with heteroskedastic outcomes it is known that even without an additional observational dataset, parametric assumptions on the outcome mean functions can improve the efficiency bound for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ (Tan, 2007), including when the propensity score is constant.

## 3 Constructing one-step estimators

Suppose $\varphi=\varphi(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ is an influence function for an RAL estimator of $\tau$ in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . Then techniques like one-step adjustment of an initial estimator $\hat{\tau}$ , solving the estimating equation $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\varphi(W_{i};\tau,\hat{\eta})=0$ for $\tau$ (where $\hat{\eta}$ is an initial estimate of the nuisance parameters $\eta^{*}$ ), and targeted minimum loss estimation (Hines et al., 2022) are all well-studied options to construct an estimator with influence function $\varphi$ .

Our focus is on providing precise conditions under which one-step adjustment, which most directly utilizes the structure of Section 2, yields an estimator that in fact achieves the efficiency bound in our models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ (i.e., has influence function equal to the EIF). We emphasize that while most attention has been placed on one-step adjustment of non-RAL estimators in nonparametric models to gain $N^{1/2}$ consistency, here we propose one-step adjustment of RAL estimators in our proper semiparametric models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , where there is typically than one possible influence function.

Let $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ be the influence function of an initial RAL estimator $\hat{\tau}$ in the semiparametric model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , as in Section 2.1. Expanding the definition of the nuisance parameters $\eta^{*}$ if necessary, let $\varphi=\varphi(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ be the desired influence function of an RAL estimator of $\tau$ (in our context, generally the EIF). By Theorem 1, we can write $\varphi=\varphi_{0}-g$ where $g=g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . Since $\tau^{*}$ and $\eta^{*}$ are not known, we need to plug in initial estimates $\hat{\tau}$ and $\hat{\eta}$ . Ensuring this initial plug-in procedure does not affect the first-order asymptotics of the one-step estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{os}}=\hat{\tau}-N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}g(W_{i};\hat{\tau},\hat{\eta})$ requires that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:g_{h}at_{m}inus_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}g(W_{i};\hat{\tau},\hat{\eta})-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

One challenge with satisfying (25) is that the nuisance parameters $\eta^{*}$ are typically infinite dimensional, and thus need to be estimated nonparametrically to avoid additional modeling assumptions. A popular approach to weaken the conditions needed for (25) to hold with nonparametric nuisance estimates is cross-fitting. Cross-fitting entails partitioning the observation indices $1,\ldots,N$ into $K$ roughly equally-sized folds $\mathcal{I}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{I}_{K}$ for some fixed $K\geqslant 2$ . Then for each fold $k=1,\ldots,K$ , we find estimates $\hat{\tau}^{(-k)}$ and $\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}$ of $\tau^{*}$ and $\eta^{*}$ , respectively, using only the observations whose indices lie outside $\mathcal{I}_{k}$ . As we will see, orthogonality properties of the influence function $\varphi$ enable the following cross-fit variant of (25) to hold even when the components of $\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}$ converge at nonparametric rates:

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:g_{h}at_{m}inus_{g}{}_{c}rossfit}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

Such a result, with sufficient conditions stated precisely in Lemma 1 below, closely follows the literature on double machine learning (Zheng and van der Laan, 2011; Chernozhukov et al., 2018).

We assume cross-fitting into $K\geqslant 2$ folds for the remainder of this section, and adopt the notation introduced in the previous paragraph in our formal results. First, we formalize the construction of our cross-fit one-step estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{os}}$ .

#### Theorem 3.

Let $\hat{\tau}_{0}$ be any RAL estimator of pathwise differentiable $\tau\in\real$ in some semiparametric model with influence function $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ . Suppose (26) holds for some $g=g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{H}^{0}$ and cross-fit estimates $\hat{\tau}^{(-k)}$ and $\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}$ of $\tau^{*}$ and $\eta^{*}$ , respectively, for $k=1,\ldots,K$ . Then

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:tau_{h}at_{o}s}\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{os}}=\hat{\tau}_{0}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right) $$

satisfies the central limit theorem $\sqrt{N}(\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{os}}-\tau^{*})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbb{E}[\varphi(W)^{2}])$ whenever the model holds, for $\varphi(\cdot)=\varphi(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ .

#### Proof.

By the definition of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{os}}$ in (27) we have

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{N}(\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{os}}-\tau^{*}) \displaystyle=\sqrt{N}(\hat{\tau}_{0}-\tau^{*})-\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\varphi_{0}(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})+o_{p}(1) $$

where by (26) and the definition of $\varphi_{0}$ , the second equality holds whenever the model holds. The result follows by the ordinary central limit theorem. ∎

Theorem 3 does not use any properties about $g$ — not even that $\varphi=\varphi_{0}-g$ is a valid influence function of an RAL estimator of $\tau$ . It also does not consider solely models of the form $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . However, the geometry of the space of influence functions of RAL estimators in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ given by Theorem 1 ensures that the condition (26) can be feasibly satisfied when $\varphi$ is in fact a valid influence function of a RAL estimator (i.e., that $g\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ ). Of course, this is necessarily the case when $\varphi=\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}$ , i.e., we are targeting the EIF.

#### Lemma 1.

Suppose the function $g=g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ is any element of the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ for some collection of outcome mean functions $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{R}$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem 2, so that we can write

$$ g(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=(y-m^{*}(r))h_{1}(r;\tau^{*},\eta^{*}) $$

where $\eta^{*}$ includes the mean function $m^{*}$ and $h_{1}^{*}(\cdot)=h_{1}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . Then equation (26) holds under the following conditions:

- • (Boundedness) There exists $C<\infty$ for which $V^{*}(r)\leqslant C$ for $P^{*}$ -almost every $r$ and both $\|h_{1}^{*}\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ and $\left\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}\right\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ where $\|f\|_{\infty,P^{*}}=\inf_{M}\textnormal{Pr}(|f(R)|\leqslant M)=1$

- • (Approximate tangency) With probability tending to 1, for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ there exists $\hat{R}^{(-k)}=\hat{R}^{(-k)}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ depending only on the observations outside fold $k$ such that the function $r\mapsto\hat{m}^{(-k)}(r)-m^{*}(r)-\hat{R}^{(-k)}(r)$ lies in the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , $\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ , and the following rate holds:

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:R_{h}at}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

(28)

- • (Rate conditions) The following rate conditions hold for all $k=1,\ldots,K$ : – (First order consistency) $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ – (Product rate condition) $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}\times\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ where $\|f\|_{2,P^{*}}=(\int f^{2}(w)dP^{*}(w))^{1/2}$ .

In the proof of Lemma 1 in Appendix A.5, we generalize Lemma 1 to cover models $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ where the experimental propensity score is known (cf. Corollary 1). The main conditions in Lemma 1 that need to be verified for a given choice of $\mathcal{M}$ are approximate tangency and the rate conditions. One can check that approximate tangency holds with $\hat{R}^{(-k)}=0$ if $m^{*}\in\mathcal{M}$ and $\hat{m}^{(-k)}\in\mathcal{M}$ for all folds $k$ with probability tending to 1, and $\mathcal{M}$ is a closed linear space. Otherwise, approximate tangency can be established (with generally nonzero remainders $\hat{R}^{(-k)}$ ) via Taylor expansion in appropriately smooth models such as $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ , provided that the outcome mean function estimates $\hat{m}^{(-k)}$ lie in $\mathcal{M}$ . The rate conditions required in Lemma 1 are standard in the double machine learning literature. Substantial work has established precise conditions under which they hold for particular nonparametric estimators (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Benkeser and van der Laan, 2016; Schuler et al., 2024).

## 4 Some specific novel efficient estimators

We are now ready to put everything together to specify novel one-step efficient estimators of the average treatment effects $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ in the models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ that assume linear confounding bias and outcome-mediated selection bias, respectively.

In Appendix B.4, we show that the EIF $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ in the linear confounding bias model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ in terms of any initial influence function $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ of an RAL estimator of $\tau$ is given by

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:eif_{4}}\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-h(r;\eta^{*})\nu(x;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle h(r;\eta) \displaystyle=\frac{sz}{p(x)e(x)}-\frac{s(1-z)}{p(x)(1-e(x))}-\frac{(1-s)z}{(1-p(x))q(x)}+\frac{(1-s)(1-z)}{(1-p(x))(1-q(x))} \displaystyle I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=\int\varphi_{0}(w;\tau,\eta)(y-m(r))h(r;\eta)dP_{(S,Z,Y)\mid X}(s,z,y;x) \displaystyle\nu(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=p(x)e(x)\frac{I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})+\lambda(\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})^{\top}\psi(x)}{\Sigma(x;\eta)} \displaystyle\Sigma(x;\eta) \displaystyle=V_{11}(x)+\frac{V_{10}(x)e(x)}{1-e(x)}+\frac{V_{01}(x)p(x)e(x)}{(1-p(x))q(x)}+\frac{V_{00}(x)p(x)e(x)}{(1-p(x))(1-q(x))} \displaystyle\lambda(\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=-\left(\int\frac{p(x)e(x)}{\Sigma(x;\eta)}\psi(x)\psi(x)^{\top}dP_{X}(x)\right)^{-1}\int\frac{I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})p(x)e(x)}{\Sigma(x;\eta)}\psi(x)dP_{X}(x) $$

for $\eta=\eta(P)$ including the nuisance functions $(p(\cdot),e(\cdot),m(\cdot),q(\cdot),V(\cdot))$ along with any other functionals that are needed to compute

$$ I(x;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\nu_{0})=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})(Y-m^{*}(R))h(R;\eta^{*})\mid X=x]. $$

Applying the construction (27) to the differences

$$ g(\cdot;\tau,\eta)=\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}(\cdot;\tau,\eta)-\varphi_{0}(\cdot;\tau,\eta)=h(r;\eta)\nu(x;\tau,\eta)(y-m(r)) $$

gives the efficient cross-fit one-step estimators

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}=\hat{\tau}_{0}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}h\Big(R_{i};\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\Big)\nu\Big(X_{i};\hat{\eta}^{(-k)},\hat{\tau}_{0},\varphi_{0}\Big)\Big(Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\Big). $$

where $\hat{\tau}_{0}$ is any initial RAL estimator with influence function $\varphi_{0}$ . Taking $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ gives efficient estimators for the estimands $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}},\tau_{\textnormal{obs}},\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , respectively. In that case, $\hat{\tau}_{0}$ can be a cross-fit AIP(S)W estimator obtained by solving the estimating equations

$$ \displaystyle N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\varphi_{0}(W_{i};\tau;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)})=0 $$

for $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ . We remind the reader that these AIP(S)W estimators are efficient in the nonparametric model. For convenience in computing (35) for the estimands $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}},\tau_{\textnormal{obs}},\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , note

$$ \displaystyle I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{V_{11}(x)}{e(x)}+\frac{V_{10}(x)}{1-e(x)}\right) \displaystyle I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}) \displaystyle=\frac{\rho(1-p(x))}{p(x)(1-\rho)}I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}),\quad I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}})=\frac{\rho}{p(x)}I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}). $$

Similarly, by (23) we can compute efficient cross-fit one-step estimators

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}=\hat{\tau}_{0}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}f\left(R_{i};\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)\zeta\left(X_{i};\hat{\eta}^{(-k)},\hat{\tau}_{0},\varphi_{0}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right) $$

in the outcome-mediated selection bias model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}$ , where $\eta(\cdot)=(p(\cdot),e(\cdot),m(\cdot),q(\cdot))$ . For convenience in computing estimators for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , we write

$$ \displaystyle\zeta(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}) \displaystyle=\frac{\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}(x))V_{11}(x)+\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}(x))\frac{e(x)}{1-e(x)}V_{10}(x)}{\rho e(x)D(x;\eta)} \displaystyle\zeta(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}) \displaystyle=\frac{\rho(1-p(x))}{(1-\rho)p(x)}\zeta(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}),\quad\zeta(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}})=\frac{\rho}{p(x)}\zeta(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}) $$

where $V_{sz}(x)=m_{sz}(x)(1-m_{sz}(x))$ for $(s,z)\in\{0,1\}^{2}$ since $Y\in\{0,1\}$ and

$$ \displaystyle D(x;\eta) \displaystyle=V_{11}(x)(\ell^{\prime}(m_{11}(x)))^{2}+\frac{e(x)}{1-e(x)}V_{10}(x)(\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}(x)))^{2} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{p(x)e(x)}{(1-p(x))q(x)}(\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}(x)))^{2}V_{01}(x)+(\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}(x))^{2}V_{00}(x)\frac{p(x)e(x)}{(1-p(x))(1-q(x))}. $$

Of course, the efficiency of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ and $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ requires that (26) holds. In Appendix C we provide specific primitive conditions that are sufficient for the conditions of Lemma 1 (and thus (26)) to hold. The main non-regularity requirement in these conditions is that the cross-fit outcome mean function estimates $\hat{m}^{(-k)}$ lie in $\mathcal{M}$ .

We also argue in Appendix B.5 that for the estimands $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , any efficient estimators in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ (for any $\mathcal{M}$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem 2) is also efficient in the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . In other words, knowledge of the experimental propensity score does not enable asymptotic variance reductions for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ under any outcome mean function restrictions.

## 5 Simulations

We study the finite-sample performance of our efficient estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ from (37) for the estimands $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , and $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ under outcome-mediated selection bias in two numerical simulation scenarios. All code and data to reproduce these results and those of the next section can be found at https://github.com/hli90722/combining_experimental_observational. We compare performance with both baseline AIP(S)W estimators and the control variate estimators proposed by Guo et al. (2022). Asymptotically, we know our efficient estimators must dominate the control variate estimators, which in turn dominate the AIP(S)W estimators as shown in Guo et al. (2022).

The first simulation scenario is identical to that considered in Section 6 of Guo et al. (2022). We call it the “discrete” scenario, as it has two covariates $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ which are i.i.d. Bern(0.5), with treatment and binary outcomes generated according to logistic models. The second simulation setting is a “continuous” scenario where $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ are independent uniformly distributed random variables on $[-1,1]$ , and there are interaction terms in the logistic models generating treatment and outcomes. See Appendix D for the exact data generating processes. In both scenarios, some of the observations are subject to strong outcome-mediated selection where cases ( $Y=1$ ) are included with probability 0.9 and controls ( $Y=0$ ) are included with probability 0.1. These observations form a synthetic biased observational dataset of size $m=3000$ . The remaining observations are not subject to selection and have a size $n_{\textnormal{rct}}\in\{300,600,1000,3000\}$ . This selection process is identical to that considered in Guo et al. (2022).

In both scenarios, the RCT propensity score $e$ is considered known; this does not change the efficiency bound, as stated at the end of the previous section. In the discrete scenario, the nuisance functions $m$ , $p$ , and $q$ are estimated by the appropriate sample averages with 1 and 2 added to the numerator and denominator, respectively. In the continuous scenario, we use multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS; Friedman (1991)) in $X$ with logit link and final terms chosen via generalized cross validation as implemented by the earth package in the R language (Milborrow, 2011) to fit the regressions defining the nuisance functions $m_{10}$ , $m_{01}$ , $m_{00}$ , $p$ , and $q$ . All MARS regressions are cross-fit with $K=5$ folds. For stability, we truncate each MARS prediction to the interval $[1/\sqrt{n},1-1/\sqrt{n}]$ for $n$ the number of observations used to fit the corresponding model. As a reminder, to ensure the efficiency of our one-step estimators, we must enforce (4). Hence we set

$$ \hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}(x)=\ell^{-1}\left(\ell\left(\hat{m}_{10}^{(-k)}(x)\right)+\ell\left(\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(x)\right)-\ell\left(\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(x)\right)\right),\quad k=1,\ldots,K. $$

We compute our baseline AIPSW estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ by solving (36). Our efficient one-step estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ are computed using (37) with $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ as the initial estimator $\hat{\tau}_{0}$ . We also use $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ as the baseline estimator to construct the control variate estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ of Guo et al. (2022), and follow that paper’s guidance for choosing control variate(s) and computing the adjustment term (see Appendix E for more details). Their guidance is not based on asymptotic variance considerations, and we note that using an efficient estimator eliminates the need to choose specific control variates. Finally, to evaluate the finite sample impacts of estimating the nuisance functions on estimator performance, we also consider oracle variants of all estimators that plug in the true nuisance functions $\eta^{*}$ .

From Tables 2 and 3, we see the oracle one step estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ has higher relative efficiency (i.e. lower MSE) than the corresponding oracle control variate estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ for all three estimands, all RCT sizes, and both simulation scenarios (discrete and continuous). Relative efficiency for $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ and $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ is defined as the MSE of the baseline $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ divided by the MSE of the estimator. The computation is done separately for oracle variants of the estimators and feasible ones (i.e., those that estimate the nuisance functions as described above). We find that estimating the nuisance functions leads to a similar degree of performance deterioration between the oracle and feasible versions for all estimators in the discrete simulations. In the continuous scenario where the nuisance estimates are harder to compute, the oracle and feasible relative efficiencies of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ are quite similar. This suggests that the control variate estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ suffers a similar amount of performance degradation from nuisance estimation as the baseline estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ . By contrast, the one-step efficient estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ exhibits a notable relative efficiency decline between the oracle and feasible variants, particularly with smaller sample sizes. This suggests that the one-step efficient estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ is more sensitive to poor nuisance estimation in finite samples than the baseline and control variate estimators. Nevertheless, the feasible efficient estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}$ has much lower MSE (10-40% reduction) than the feasible control variate estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ across all estimands, RCT sizes, and scenarios. This suggests the asymptotic variance gap between the control variate and efficient estimators is quite large.

## 6 Data example

We now consider a real data example based on estimating $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ in data from the Tennessee Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) study. This is inspired by Kallus et al. (2018), who use the same dataset and the linear confounding bias assumption (3) to study treatment effect hetereogeneity. The Tennessee STAR study was a large RCT designed to investigate whether small class sizes improve test outcomes. For simplicity, we only consider three binary covariates: gender, race (white or non-white), and whether the student received free lunch in grade 1. We also include birth date as a continuous covariate.

Following Kallus et al. (2018), the outcome is the sum of listening, reading, and math scores (divided by 100) at the end of first grade. We randomly subsample 1405 students from rural or inner-city schools to be our RCT dataset, and generate an observational dataset (with different covariate distribution) by combining the observations from the remaining 1406 students from rural or inner-city schools with 1407 students from urban or suburban schools. We randomly set aside 30% (1125) of the observations in the observational dataset as a “validation set” to represent the target population. In the remaining 1688 observations, we synthetically introduce confounding by reducing all outcomes above the median by the difference between the average outcome above the median and the average outcome below the median. The nuisance functions $m_{10}$ , $m_{01}$ , $m_{00}$ , $p$ , and $q$ are computed using MARS and cross-fitting ( $K=5$ ) in the same way as in the simulations of Section 5, except that for the outcome mean function estimates, we now use the identity link and do not truncate. The three binary predictors are encoded as 0 or 1. We enforce (3) by setting

$$ \hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}(x)=\hat{m}_{10}^{(-k)}(x)+\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(x)-\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(x)+\psi(x)^{\top}\hat{\theta},\quad k=1,\ldots,K $$

where $\psi(x)$ consists of an intercept term and each of the covariates (additively) and

$$ \hat{\theta}=\argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}\left(Y_{i}\left[\frac{Z_{i}}{e^{*}}-\frac{1-Z_{i}}{1-e^{*}}\right]-\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-\psi(X_{i})^{\top}\theta\right)^{2} $$

following Kallus et al. (2018), where $e^{*}$ is the known constant RCT propensity score. The astute reader might notice that $\hat{\theta}$ is not cross-fit so this makes $\hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}$ not cross-fit either. This does not violate the theoretical guarantees of efficiency of our estimators, however, since $\theta\mapsto\psi(x)^{\top}\theta$ is a Donsker class. The variance functions $V_{11}$ , $V_{10}$ , $V_{01}$ , $V_{00}$ are computed using a generalized linear model with logarithmic link predicting the squared residuals $(Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{(-k(i))}(R_{i}))^{2}$ from the covariates. This is similar to Yang et al. (2024). Finally, the estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ and the baseline AIPSW estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ are computed on a set of “training observations” consisting of a randomly sampled fraction $\xi\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,1\}$ of our RCT dataset along with the entire confounded observational dataset of 1688 subjects. The one-step estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ is derived assuming (3) holds with $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ as the initial estimator $\hat{\tau}_{0}$ , with influence function $\varphi_{0}$ .

Taking an AIPSW estimate of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ computed via (36) using the validation set to be the true estimand $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ for evaluation purposes, we observe substantial precision gains from using the efficient one-step estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ instead of the baseline AIPSW estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ for all RCT sample sizes $\xi$ . The relative variance improvement from using the efficient one-step estimator appears to generally increase with $\xi$ . When the full RCT dataset is used ( $\xi=1$ ), we observe a 75% variance reduction in 1000 bootstrap replicates, though there is substantial uncertainty in that estimate (Table 4). Since this is a real data example, we do not know (3) to hold, yet assuming (3) (as $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ does) appears to introduce a negligible amount of bias into $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ (Fig. 1). In other words, the MSE reductions in Table 4 from using $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}$ can be attributed almost entirely to variance reduction, and are minimally offset by bias.

## 7 Discussion

We have provided a general semiparametric theory for supervised learning under generic restrictions on the outcome mean function. Many assumptions used for data fusion in the recent causal inference literature are covered by this theory, which we hope provides a valuable unifying perspective. Sometimes these assumptions have not been fully leveraged for maximal variance reduction, as illustrated by the inefficiency of control variate approaches in the outcome-mediated selection bias setting. This paper has sought to present a streamlined way to derive fully efficient estimators under a large class of restrictions on outcome mean functions, while also providing additional mathematical insights into the nature of efficiency bounds under such restrictions.

Our setting does not handle all types of data fusion restrictions that have been of interest. For instance, some authors have imposed structure on quantile treatment effects (Athey et al., 2023) or shape restrictions on the density function of a continuous outcome (Li and Luedtke, 2023), which cannot be formulated as restrictions on the outcome mean function. Other recent work (Li and Luedtke, 2023; Li et al., 2025) has also aimed to provide general data fusion frameworks guided by semiparametric efficiency. These frameworks, however, do not cover many settings of interest that can be cast as restrictions on outcome mean functions. For instance, consider our data fusion setting with $R=(S,Z,X)$ and suppose $Y\in\{0,1\}$ , so that the outcome mean function in fact specifies the entire conditional distribution of $Y$ given $(S,Z,X)$ . Then for the observational dataset to be used at all in estimating any parameter depending on the conditional distribution of $Y\mid Z,X,S=1$ (i.e. the experimental outcome distribution), Li and Luedtke (2023) require an “alignment” assumption that amounts to $m(s,z,x)$ being independent of $s$ . The “weak alignment” assumption of Li et al. (2025) weakens this to allow

$$ \ell(m(1,z,x))=\ell(m(0,z,x))+\beta^{\top}\psi(z,x) $$

for some known low-dimensional basis expansion $\psi$ . If $x$ is continuous, however, this is not flexible enough to cover the outcome-mediated selection bias setting of Example 5, which is equivalent to $\ell(m(1,z,x))-\ell(m(0,z,x))=f(x)$ , $z=0,1$ for arbitrary $f\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ . Conversely, if $Y$ is continuous, the weak alignment assumption induces restrictions on higher moments of the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $R$ which cannot be expressed solely as restrictions on the outcome mean function.

Asymptotic efficiency also has some limitations as an objective for precise inference in finite samples. Based on the simulations in Section 5, the one-step efficient estimators proposed in this work can have worse relative finite sample performance than asymptotics might suggest, which we attribute to the need to estimate additional nuisance functions relative to the baselines. Thus, we believe extensions of ideas from the nonparametric literature to improve nuisance estimation such as pooling the datasets (Gagnon-Bartsch et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2023) and Riesz regression (Klosin, 2021; Chernozhukov et al., 2022; Lee and Schuler, 2025) may be useful to extend to models with outcome mean function restrictions. Substantial recent work has also exhibited finite sample benefits to non-regular estimators combining experimental and observational datasets (Chen et al., 2021; Cheng and Cai, 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Dang et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2025; Rosenman et al., 2023). While such estimators are, in some sense, more robust in that they don’t require assumptions on outcome mean functions, Oberst et al. (2023) showed that many of these estimators will end up performing worse than the efficiency bound in the nonparametric model when the bias is larger than some constant multiple of $N^{-1/2}$ (Oberst et al., 2023). Further work is needed to more precisely understand when such estimators may be beneficial.

## Appendix A Proofs

Here we collect the proofs of the results stated in the main text.

### A.1 Preliminaries

First, we state and prove some useful elementary results in asymptotic statistics.

#### Lemma 2.

Let $X_{n}$ be a sequence of random vectors and $\{\mathcal{F}_{n},n\geqslant 1\}$ be a sequence of $\sigma$ -algebras such that $\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|X_{n}\|\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\bigr]=o_{p}(1)$ . Then $X_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 2.

Fixing $M>0$ , we have $M\bm{1}(\|X_{n}\|>M)\leqslant\|X_{n}\|$ for all $n$ . Taking conditional expectations given $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ on both sides we have

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:cond_{m}arkov}P\bigl(\|X_{n}\|>M\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\bigr)\leqslant M^{-1}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|X_{n}\|\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\bigr]. $$

Thus if $\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|X_{n}\|\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\bigr]=o_{p}(1)$ we have $\textnormal{Pr}(\|X_{n}\|>M\mid\mathcal{F}_{n})=o_{p}(1)$ as well. But $\textnormal{Pr}(\|X_{n}\|>M\mid\mathcal{F}_{n})$ is uniformly bounded so its expectation converges to zero, i.e., $\textnormal{Pr}(\|X_{n}\|>M)=o(1)$ . Since $M>0$ was arbitrary we conclude that $X_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 3.

Let $\{\hat{f}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , $\{f_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , $\{\hat{g}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , and $\{g_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be sequences of $P$ -square integrable functions with $\|\hat{f}_{n}-f_{n}\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(a_{n})$ and $\|\hat{g}_{n}-g_{n}\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(b_{n})$ for some sequences $a_{n}\downarrow 0$ , $b_{n}\downarrow 0$ . Further suppose that there exists $C<\infty$ independent of $n$ for which $\|\hat{f}_{n}\|_{\infty}+\|g_{n}\|_{\infty}\leqslant C$ for all $n\geqslant 1$ . Then $\|\hat{f}_{n}\hat{g}_{n}-f_{n}g_{n}\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(a_{n})+o_{p}(b_{n})$ .

#### Proof.

By Minkowksi’s inequality we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{f}_{n}\hat{g}_{n}-f_{n}g_{n}\|_{2,P} \displaystyle\leqslant\|(\hat{f}_{n}-f_{n})g_{n}\|_{2,P}+\|\hat{f}_{n}(\hat{g}_{n}-g_{n})\|_{2,P} \displaystyle\leqslant C\|\hat{f}_{n}-f_{n}\|_{2,P}+C\|\hat{g}_{n}-g_{n}\|_{2,P} \displaystyle=o_{p}(a_{n})+o_{p}(b_{n}). $$

∎

#### Lemma 4.

Let $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ be i.i.d. random variables taking values in a space $\mathcal{X}$ with distribution $P$ and let $\|f\|_{2,P}=(\int f^{2}(x)dP(x))^{1/2}$ . Suppose $\hat{f}_{n}(\cdot)$ is a sequence of random measurable functions on $\mathcal{X}$ independent of $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ for which $\|\hat{f}_{n}-f\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(r_{n})$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ for some sequence $\{r_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ . Then

$$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{f}_{n}(X_{i})-f(X_{i}))^{2}}=o_{p}(r_{n}). $$

#### Proof.

Define the quantity

$$ Y_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{f}_{n}(X_{i})-f(X_{i}))^{2} $$

and note that

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{n}\mid\hat{f}_{n})=\|\hat{f}_{n}-f\|_{2,P}^{2}=o_{p}(r_{n}^{2}) $$

Then $Y_{n}=o_{p}(r_{n}^{2})$ by Lemma 2, and the result follows. ∎

#### Lemma 5.

Suppose $(A_{1},B_{1}),(A_{2},B_{2}),\ldots$ are random variables with $\mathbb{E}[A_{n}]<\infty$ for all $n\geqslant 1$ . Let $\{\mathcal{F}_{n},n\geqslant 1\}$ be a sequence of $\sigma$ -algebras such that for each $n$ , $(A_{1},\ldots,A_{n})$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ and $B_{1},\ldots,B_{n}$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ . Further assume that $\mathbb{E}[B_{i}\mid\mathcal{A}_{n}]=0$ and that there exists $C<\infty$ such that $\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{2}\mid\mathcal{A}_{n}]\leqslant C$ for all $n\geqslant 1$ , $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$ . Finally suppose that $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{2}=o_{p}(r_{n}^{2})$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ for some positive sequence $r_{n}$ . Then

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}B_{i}=o_{p}(r_{n}/\sqrt{n}). $$

#### Proof.

We have

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}B_{i}\mid\mathcal{A}_{n}\right]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\mathbb{E}[B_{i}\mid\mathcal{A}_{n}]=0 $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}B_{i}\right)^{2}\Bigg|\mathcal{A}_{n}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}B_{i}\Big|\mathcal{A}_{n}\right)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{2}\mathbb{E}[B_{i}^{2}\mid\mathcal{A}_{n}]\leqslant\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{2}=o_{p}(n^{-1}r_{n}^{2}) $$

It follows by Lemma 2 that

$$ \frac{1}{r_{n}\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}B_{i}=o_{p}(1) $$

as desired. ∎

But the condition $\sup_{0<\|a\|\leqslant b_{n}}\frac{\left|m^{(n)}\left(R;a\right)-m^{*}(R)\right|}{\|a\|}\leqslant a_{n}$ ensures that whenever $\|\gamma_{1}^{(n)}\|\leqslant\min\left(b_{n},\frac{\tilde{c}_{n}\delta}{2a_{n}}\right)$ we in fact have $\left|m^{(n)}(r;\gamma_{1}^{(n)})-m^{*}(r)\right|\leqslant\frac{\tilde{c}_{n}\delta}{2}$ , showing the existence of $c^{(n)}\left(r;\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}^{(n)}\right)$ to satisfy (43) for all $r$ and $\left(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}^{(n)}\right)$ in a neighborhood of 0.. Note that $f^{(n)}$ is indeed a valid density due to boundedness of $\bar{h}_{1}^{(n)}$ ensuring $1+\gamma_{0}\bar{h}_{1}^{(n)}(w)>0$ for all $w$ and all $\gamma_{0}$ sufficiently close to 0, while equation (43) ensures the densities $f^{(n)}$ correspond to distributions with mean functions lying in $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . Now using the quotient rule and noting we can take $c^{(n)}(r;0,0)=0$ for all $r$ by (42), we compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial f^{(n)}(y\mid r,0,0)}{\partial\gamma_{0}} \displaystyle=f^{*}(y\mid r)\bar{h}_{1}^{(n)}(w) \displaystyle\frac{\partial f^{(n)}(y\mid r;0,0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}} \displaystyle=(y-m^{*}(r))f^{*}(y\mid r)\frac{\partial c^{(n)}(r;0,0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}} $$

which are square integrable by Assumption 1. So $f^{(n)}(y\mid r;\gamma^{(n)})$ is a parametric submodel for the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $R=r$ in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ with score

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\log f^{(n)}(w;0)}{\partial\gamma^{(n)}} \displaystyle=\left(\bar{h}_{1}^{(n)}(w),(y-m^{*}(r))\frac{\partial c^{(n)}(r;0,0)}{\partial\left(\gamma_{1}^{(n)}\right)^{\top}}\right)^{\top} $$

for $\gamma^{(n)}=(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}^{(n)})$ . By taking the derivative of both sides of (43) with respect to $\gamma_{1}^{(n)}$ at $\gamma_{0}=0$ , $\gamma_{1}^{(n)}=0$ , we see that

$$ \frac{\partial c^{(n)}(r;0;0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}}V^{*}(r)=\frac{\partial m^{(n)}(r;0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}} $$

so we can rewrite

$$ (y-m^{*}(r))\frac{\partial c^{(n)}(r;0,0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}}=\frac{(y-m^{*}(r))\frac{\partial m^{(n)}(r;0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}}}{V^{*}(r)} $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle(1,c_{n}^{\top})^{\top}\frac{\partial\log f^{(n)}(w;0)}{\partial\gamma^{(n)}} \displaystyle=\bar{h}_{1}^{(n)}(w)+(y-m^{*}(r))\frac{c_{n}^{\top}\frac{\partial m^{(n)}(r;0)}{\partial\gamma_{1}^{(n)}}}{V^{*}(r)} $$

which we’ve ensured converge in mean square to

$$ \bar{h}_{1}(w)+\frac{(y-m^{*}(r))\tilde{h}_{1}(r)}{V^{*}(r)}=h_{1}(w) $$

as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . This allows us to conclude $h_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , as desired.

Having shown $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathcal{T}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2}$ with $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ as in (40) and $\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{H}_{R}^{0}$ , we are now ready to prove (8). First suppose $g$ is an element of the right-hand side of (8), so that $g(w)=h(r)(y-m^{*}(r))$ for some $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . Then for any $g_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(W)g_{1}(W)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[h(R)\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{*}(R))g_{1}(W)\mid R]]\text{ by conditioning on $R$} \displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}[h(R)m^{*}(R)\mathbb{E}[g_{1}(W)\mid R]]\text{ since $\mathbb{E}[Yg_{1}(W)\mid R]\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$} \displaystyle=0\text{ since $\mathbb{E}[g_{1}(W)\mid R]=0$}. $$

Additionally, for any $g_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{2}$ we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[g(W)g_{2}(R)]=\mathbb{E}[h(R)g_{2}(R)\mathbb{E}[Y-m^{*}(R)\mid R]]=0 $$

Hence $g\in\mathcal{T}_{1}^{\perp}\cap\mathcal{T}_{2}^{\perp}=(\mathcal{T}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2})^{\perp}$ , completing the inclusion “ $\supseteq$ ” of (8).

To show the reverse inclusion, we now fix $g\in(\mathcal{T}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2})^{\perp}$ . Since $g\in\mathcal{T}_{2}^{\perp}$ but $x\mapsto\mathbb{E}[g(W)\mid R=r]\in\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , by conditioning on $R$ we have

$$ 0=\mathbb{E}[g(W)\mathbb{E}[g(W)\mid R]]=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[g(W)\mid R])^{2}] $$

and so $\mathbb{E}[g(W)\mid R]=0$ . Next, we define

$$ \tilde{g}(w)=h(r)(y-m^{*}(r)),\quad h(r)=\frac{\int(y^{\prime}-m^{*}(r))g(r,y^{\prime})f^{*}(y\mid r)d\mu(y)}{V^{*}(r)} $$

so that $h(R)V^{*}(R)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{*}(R))g(W)\mid R]$ . Notice that $g-\tilde{g}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , since

$$ \mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}(W)\mid R]=h(R)\mathbb{E}[Y-m^{*}(R)\mid R]=0=\mathbb{E}[g(W)\mid R] $$

while

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y(g(W)-\tilde{g}(W))\mid R] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Yg(W)\mid R]-\mathbb{E}\left[Yh(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R\right] \displaystyle=h(R)V^{*}(R)-\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}h(R)\mid R] \displaystyle=0\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}} $$

where the second equality uses the fact that $\mathbb{E}[h(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R]=\mathbb{E}[h(R)g(W)\mid R]=0$ for all $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ . Since $g\in\mathcal{T}_{1}^{\perp}$ we must have

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:g_{p}erp}\mathbb{E}[g(W)(g(W)-\tilde{g}(W))]=0. $$

It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(g(W)-\tilde{g}(W))^{2}] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}^{2}(W)]-\mathbb{E}[g(W)\tilde{g}(W)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{*}(R))g(W)\mid R])^{2}(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}}{(V^{*}(R))^{2}}\right] \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}[g(W)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R]g(W)(Y-m^{*}(R))}{V^{*}(R)}\right] \displaystyle=0 $$

Hence $g(w)=\tilde{g}(w)$ . Finally we note that $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ since for any $h_{1}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[h_{1}(R)h(R)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h_{1}(R)\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{*}(R))g(W)\mid R]}{V^{*}(R)}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(Y-m^{*}(R))g(W)h_{1}(R)}{V^{*}(R)}\right] \displaystyle=0 $$

where the last equality follows since $g\in\mathcal{T}_{1}^{\perp}$ but

$$ \hat{g}(w)=\frac{(y-m^{*}(r))h_{1}(r)}{V^{*}(r)} $$

satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\hat{g}(W)\mid R]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y\hat{g}(W)\mid R]=h_{1}(R)$ so that $\hat{g}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ by definition.

### A.3 Proof of Corollary 1

We write $\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}$ as the direct sum of orthogonal subspaces $\mathcal{T}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2}$ where

$$ \mathcal{T}_{1}=\{f\in\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}\mid\mathbb{E}[f(W)\mid R]=0\},\quad\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{H}_{R}^{0}. $$

Since the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ places no restrictions on the distribution of $R$ , it follows that its semiparametric tangent space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2}$ for some $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{1}$ (this is also easy to see directly from the fact that $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{1}$ by (8)). Conversely, the experimental propensity score being known places no restriction on the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $R$ . Thus, we can write $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}=\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{1}\oplus\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}$ where $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}$ is the semiparametric tangent space for the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{N}}$ on the distribution of $R=(Z,S,X)$ , viewing $Z$ as the outcome and $(S,X)$ the covariates and letting $\mathcal{N}=\{(s,x)\mapsto se^{*}(x)+(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ so that the restriction that the mapping $(s,x)\mapsto\mathbb{E}[Z\mid S=s,X=x]\in\mathcal{N}$ amounts precisely to the experimental propensity score being known and equal to $e^{*}$ . By (8) we have

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:T_{2}{}_{p}erp_{t}ilde}\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}^{\perp}=\{(z-e^{*}(x))h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}\} $$

where $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}$ is the orthogonal complement of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}$ in $\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ and $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}^{\perp}$ denotes the orthogonal complement of $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}$ in $\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{H}_{R}^{0}$ , (not the orthogonal complement in $\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}$ ). We conclude

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\oplus\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{2}^{\perp}. $$

Thus, to prove (24) it suffices to show that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}=\{(s,x)\mapsto sh(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}. $$

To that end, we first show that $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}=\{(s,x)\mapsto(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ . To do so, note that the RHS is a closed subset of $\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ , and that an arbitrary outcome mean function parametric submodel of $\mathcal{N}$ takes the form

$$ m(s,x;\gamma)=se^{*}(x)+(1-s)h(x;\gamma) $$

where $h(x;0)=r^{*}(x)$ . For any $c$ with the same length as $\gamma$ we have

$$ c^{\top}\frac{\partial m(s,x;0)}{\partial\gamma}=(1-s)c^{\top}\frac{\partial h(x;0)}{\partial\gamma} $$

which clearly lies in the set $\{(s,x)\mapsto(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ . Hence $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}$ is contained inside this set. Conversely, given an arbitrary element $g$ given by $g(s,x)=(1-s)h(x)$ in this set, we can consider the univariate submodels

$$ m_{n}(s,x;\gamma)=se^{*}(x)+(1-s)(q^{*}(x)+\gamma h_{n}(x)) $$

for a sequence of bounded functions $h_{n}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ converging in mean square to $h$ . Note the validity of each of these submodels for $\gamma$ in a neighborhood of zero uses the fact that $h_{n}$ is bounded and $\delta<q^{*}(x)<1-\delta$ for all $x$ and some $\delta>0$ . With $\partial m_{n}(s,x;\gamma)/\partial\gamma\Big|_{\gamma=0}$ converging to $g(s,x)$ in mean square, we conclude $g\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}$ , and indeed $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}=\{(s,x)\mapsto(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ . Given this, it is then straightforward to verify that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}=\{(s,x)\mapsto sh(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\} $$

upon recalling that $s(1-s)=0$ .

### A.4 Proof of Corollary 2

It suffices to show that $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ is the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ in the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , since $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{R}}$ and hence the semiparametric bound for $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ must be sandwiched between the bounds for $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ and the nonparametric model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{R}}$ . To do so, by Theorem 1 it suffices to show that $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}\in(\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp})^{\perp}=\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ .

Fix an arbitrary element $g\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . By Theorem 2, we can write $g(w)=h(r)(y-m^{*}(r))+s\tilde{h}(x)(z-e^{*}(x))$ for some $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ and $\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ . For each $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ , with $\Delta(z,x,y;\eta)$ as in Proposition 1, we define

$$ \displaystyle\phi(r;f) \displaystyle=h(r)\mathbb{E}[((\rho^{*})^{-1}S\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})+f(R))(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R=r] \displaystyle=h(r)\left(\frac{sz}{\rho^{*}e^{*}}\mathbb{E}[(Y-m_{11}^{*}(X))^{2}\mid R]-\frac{s(1-z)}{\rho^{*}(1-e^{*})}\mathbb{E}[(Y-m_{10}^{*}(X))^{2}\mid R]\right) \displaystyle=h(r)(\rho^{*})^{-1}(c_{1}sz-c_{0}s(1-z)) $$

where $c_{1}=\sigma_{1}^{2}/e^{*}$ and $c_{0}=\sigma_{0}^{2}/(1-e^{*})$ , and the second equality uses the fact that $f(r)\mathbb{E}[Y-m^{*}(R)\mid R]=0$ . Note $\phi(r;f)$ is independent of $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ and by the assumption of the theorem, $r\mapsto(\rho^{*})^{-1}(c_{1}sz-c_{0}s(1-z))\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . With $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ we conclude that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:phi}\mathbb{E}[\phi(R;f)]=0,\quad\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}. $$

Next, we note that for any $\bar{g}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*})(\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})+\bar{g}(X))\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*})\mathbb{E}(\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})\mid S=1,Z,X)\right] \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}[S\tilde{h}(X)\bar{g}(X)\mathbb{E}(Z-e^{*}\mid S=1,X)] \displaystyle=0 $$

Finally, we put together (46) and (47) to show that $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ must be orthogonal to our arbitrary chosen function $g\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . By iterated expectations, defining $f(r)=s(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*})/\rho^{*}$ we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0,rct}(W;\tau_{rct}^{*},\eta^{*})g(W)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*};\eta^{*})(h(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))+S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*}))] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[h(R)\mathbb{E}(\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*};\eta^{*})(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R] \displaystyle\quad+(\rho^{*})^{-1}\mathbb{E}[S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*})(\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})+m_{11}^{*}(X)-m_{10}^{*}(X)-\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*})] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\phi(S,Z,X;f)]+0\text{ by~\eqref{eq:h_tilde_iota} with $\bar{g}(X)=m_{11}^{*}(X)-m_{10}^{*}(X)-\tau^{*}_{\textnormal{rct}}$} \displaystyle=0\text{ by~\eqref{eq:phi}}. $$

### A.5 Proof of Lemma 1

As indicated in the main text, here we prove a stronger version of Lemma 1 that is applicable to models of the form $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ where the experimental propensity score is known, as considered in Corollary 1.

#### Lemma.

Suppose the function $g=g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ is any element of the space $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ for some collection of outcome mean functions $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{R}$ satisfying the conditions of Corollary 1, so that we can write

$$ g(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=(y-m^{*}(r))h_{1}(r;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})+s(z-e^{*}(x))h_{2}(x;\tau^{*},\eta^{*}) $$

where $\eta^{*}$ includes the mean function $m^{*}$ , $h_{1}^{*}(\cdot)=h_{1}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , and $h_{2}^{*}(\cdot)=h_{2}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ . Then equation (26) holds under the following conditions:

- • (Boundedness) There exists $C<\infty$ for which $V^{*}(r)\leqslant C$ for $P^{*}$ -almost every $r$ and both $\|h_{i}^{*}\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ and $\left\|\hat{h}_{i}^{(-k)}\right\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ for $i=1,2$

- • (Approximate tangency) With probability tending to 1, for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ there exists $\hat{R}^{(-k)}=\hat{R}^{(-k)}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ depending only on the observations outside fold $k$ such that the function $r\mapsto\hat{m}^{(-k)}(r)-m^{*}(r)-\hat{R}^{(-k)}(r)$ lies in the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , $\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ , and the following rate holds:

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:R_{h}at_{g}eneralized}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

(48)

- • (Rate conditions) The following rate conditions hold for all $k=1,\ldots,K$ : – (First order consistency) $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}-h_{2}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ – (Product rate condition) $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}\times\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ .

Lemma 1 follows immediately from the modified Lemma above since $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\supseteq\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , and for any $g\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ we can apply the modified Lemma with $h_{2}=h_{2}^{(-k)}=0$ .

Writing

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}{N}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*}) $$

we see it suffices to fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and show

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

We have

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=a_{k}+b_{k} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle a_{k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-(Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i}))h_{1}^{*}(R_{i}) \displaystyle b_{k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}(Z_{i}-e^{*}(X_{i}))\left(\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-h_{2}^{*}(X_{i})\right). $$

We further expand

$$ a_{k}=a_{1k}+a_{2k}+a_{3k} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle a_{1k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)h_{1}^{*}(R_{i}) \displaystyle a_{2k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i}))\left(\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\right) \displaystyle a_{3k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)\left(\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\right) $$

$$ \Bigg|\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\Bigg|\leqslant C\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

by (48) and the boundedness condition $\|h_{1}^{*}\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ . Hence $a_{1k}=\tilde{a}_{1k}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ where

$$ \tilde{a}_{1k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})+m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)h_{1}^{*}(R_{i}). $$

Furthermore, whenever $\hat{R}^{(-k)}$ exists, we have that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})+m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}\right]=0 $$

for each $i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ ; here $\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}$ is the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by the observations outside fold $k$ , and the preceding display holds since $\hat{R}^{(-k)}+m^{*}-m^{(-k)}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ (recall $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ is assumed to be a linear space, hence it is closed under multiplication by negative 1) but $h_{1}^{*}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . With the summands in $\tilde{a}_{1k}$ i.i.d. across $i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ conditional on $\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}$ , we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{a}_{1k}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\int\left(\hat{R}^{(-k)}(r)+m^{*}(r)-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(r)\right)^{2}(h_{1}^{*}(r))^{2}dP^{*}(w) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C^{2}}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\left\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}+m^{*}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}\right\|_{2,P^{*}}^{2}\text{ by boundedness of $h_{1}^{*}$} \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1}) $$

since $|\mathcal{I}_{k}|^{-1}=O(N^{-1})$ while

$$ \|\hat{R}^{(-k)}+m^{*}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}\leqslant\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1). $$

by Minkowski’s inequality and the rate conditions $\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ and $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ . We conclude by Lemma 2 that $\tilde{a}_{1k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ and hence $a_{1k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ as well.

Next, we show $a_{2k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ . Note that $\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)},\mathcal{F}_{R}^{(k)}\right]=0$ for all $i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ where $\mathcal{F}_{R}^{(k)}$ is the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by $(R_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}$ .
